entries.title: A game in front of the crowd
entries.event_semantics: Public demonstration at the 1950 Canadian National Exhibition. Kates’s retrospective recollection differs by a year; institutional chronology is retained and the discrepancy is explicit.
entries.summary: Kates connected experimental electronics with a contest anyone could follow.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Kates reached computing through several kinds of machinery. In his 1992 interview, he remembered studying mathematics and physics in Toronto while also working at Rogers Majestic. Radio tubes were part of his paid employment; experimental computing became another place to apply that knowledge. This was not a games company recruiting a games designer. A university researcher and an electronics manufacturer were approaching a shared technical problem. Bertie emerged from that connection, before anyone involved needed a videogame department or a market category to explain the project.

The machine presented two views of the contest: a small board for the player and a larger illuminated board for the watching crowd. Kates recalled adjustable difficulty and a version of tic-tac-toe that could punish a mistaken move. He also remembered Harry Stein helping with construction at Rogers. Kates dated this exhibition encounter to 1951. People had to see whose turn it was, understand the result and believe that another attempt might go differently. The public display made a private decision visible to everyone standing nearby.

Rogers hoped the installation would draw attention to the Additron, a binary adder tube. The Canada Science and Technology Museum’s research places it within efforts to build UTEC at the University of Toronto. Technical difficulties kept the component from becoming part of that full-scale computer; Bertie instead became its special-purpose demonstration. For the manufacturer, the game advertised an electronic device. For a visitor, the device disappeared behind the much simpler question of where to place the next mark. Those purposes occupied the same cabinet.

The museum monograph dates Bertie’s Canadian National Exhibition appearance to 1950 and reproduces a photograph in its account of early Canadian computing. Its detailed caption traces that image through John Vardalas’s research to a Rogers Majestic publication. That chain matters: the picture is evidence of an installation, not a newly made reconstruction or an openly licensed museum illustration. Beside the game, the Additron belongs to a larger history of machines that did not develop as planned. The record shows both the public attraction and the engineering ambition behind it.

entries.title: The computer shows its working
entries.event_semantics: Festival of Britain demonstration in 1951. Exact opening-day claims are not adopted pending chronology reconciliation.
entries.summary: A game gave Ferranti visitors a way to inspect computation.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Ferranti took a purpose-built Nim-playing machine to the 1951 Festival of Britain. John Bennett proposed the project, and engineer Raymond Stuart-Williams turned the proposal into working hardware. The familiar game gave visitors a way into an unfamiliar subject: automatic computation. A person could make a legal move, wait for the reply and understand the consequence without learning the machine’s circuitry first. Nimrod therefore belonged to an exhibition about technology as well as a history of play. Its public audience was part of the engineering brief, rather than an accidental discovery after construction.

Ferranti’s original guide explains how controls represented match heaps. Instead of moving counters by hand, the player pressed a numbered button on the control panel to leave a chosen amount in a heap, then asked the computer to respond. Lamps displayed the position. The arrangement translated a rule into an interface: a button expressed a choice in the game. The same written guide described input, storage and output, using the contest as a practical example of how those parts could work together.

Nimrod could display a sequence of instructions as it selected a move. Illuminated steps and arrows exposed part of the calculation instead of hiding everything behind the answer. This was a different ambition from giving a machine a mysterious personality. Ferranti’s booklet warned that describing computers as brains could make their operation seem unknowable. The game offered an inspectable problem. Visitors might enjoy winning or losing, but the demonstration also invited them to follow how a result was produced. A visible process was part of what Ferranti wanted to sell.

A surviving 1951 first-edition manual is catalogued by the Science Museum Group as object 2014-500. Closed, the paper booklet measures 179 by 103 millimetres: a small thing a visitor could carry away from a very large machine. That difference in scale is useful. The installation needed a public setting and a demonstrator; the booklet could continue the explanation afterwards. The museum record identifies the publication and its material form without pretending that the machine survives inside it. To reconstruct the encounter, the hardware history and this modest printed guide have to be read together.

entries.title: A telephone dial becomes a game control
entries.event_semantics: Douglas’s EDSAC game, circa 1952; no exact completion day or unverified thesis-topic claim is asserted.
entries.summary: Douglas adapted EDSAC’s controls for a familiar exchange of moves.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: At Cambridge around 1952, Alexander Douglas used EDSAC to play noughts and crosses. A rotary telephone dial supplied the player’s choices, while a small cathode-ray display showed the board. The Computer History Museum describes a version that allowed either the person or the computer to make the opening move. There was no domestic console to unpack and no arcade cabinet waiting for a coin. The encounter took place around a research machine. A familiar paper game made the exchange between an instruction, a calculation and a visible answer easy to recognize.

EDSAC had been built to serve Cambridge researchers. Maurice Wilkes led the project, Bill Renwick directed construction, and David Wheeler contributed methods that helped people use it. The National Museum of Computing describes a practical service, rather than a machine reserved for specialists. Douglas’s game sat inside that larger undertaking. Before the screen could become a board, other people had designed an environment in which a program could be entered, run and tested. The apparently small interaction depended on that shared work.

The replica project’s simulator guide explains that EDSAC’s monitor tubes could reveal the contents of parts of its memory. They were working instruments, not screens originally built around entertainment. The same guide opens with Douglas’s game and tells a present-day user to select OXO and enter moves through the simulated dial. That pairing makes the adaptation tangible. What looks like a minimal board is also a different use for an existing display. The simulator preserves the awkwardness of the interface rather than replacing it with the controls of a modern game.

The museum’s reconstruction project aims to reproduce EDSAC as it stood in 1951, when it entered everyday service. The original computer has not survived intact. A working reconstruction can make timing, maintenance and operation understandable, but it also embodies later research and decisions. When we show Douglas’s game today, the caption needs to identify that setting. The historical program, its simulated or reconstructed machine and the player’s present encounter are related layers of evidence. Keeping them separate makes the demonstration more informative, rather than less impressive.

entries.title: Two controls at a laboratory open day
entries.event_semantics: Brookhaven visitors’ day demonstration on 18 October 1958; the feature also distinguishes the later 2008 reconstruction.
entries.summary: Two laboratory colleagues turned visitors into players using available equipment.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Brookhaven’s visitors’ day gave William Higinbotham a problem: how could a laboratory exhibit invite visitors to participate? On 18 October 1958, visitors encountered an electronic tennis game. Higinbotham designed the arrangement, and technician Robert Dvorak built it with him. An analog computer and an oscilloscope became the means of play. Their purpose here was unusually direct. Two visitors could take the controls and see a ball move because of their own decisions, rather than listen to an explanation of what the equipment might do.

Each player held a separate controller. Turning a dial changed the angle, and a button sent the ball back into motion. The oscilloscope presented the court from the side, with the ball crossing a net between opponents. Its small display needed to make several things legible: the court, the moving point and the result of a hit. Brookhaven’s account describes switching circuitry that combined those elements into the image. The apparatus was not imitating a future television console. It was making a shared physical activity out of the available tools.

For the game’s 2008 anniversary, Brookhaven presented a reconstruction made by Peter Takacs, Gene Von Achen, Paul O’Connor and Scott Coburn. They used Higinbotham’s plans and sought period components, including relays and germanium transistors. The original vacuum-tube analog computer, however, had to be simulated with modern integrated circuits. The result could reproduce the interaction without being materially identical to the 1958 installation. That distinction belongs beside any photograph of the rebuilt game. Its simplicity conceals the original engineering and the research needed to make it playable again.

The demonstration needed repair. Brookhaven’s contemporary report describes a fault after roughly two hours: the court line vanished from the screen. Takacs consulted the plans, O’Connor found the required oscillator chip, and Von Achen replaced the damaged part. The game was working again within 25 minutes. This preservation story has named people and a specific repair. Keeping an early game alive meant understanding the circuit well enough to diagnose what the missing line implied. The demonstration preserved an activity, but it also depended on the ability to maintain it.

entries.title: A game improved by the next pair of hands
entries.event_semantics: Collaborative PDP-1 game development in 1962, followed separately by the museum’s 2004–2005 restoration.
entries.summary: A collaborative program depended on another collective effort to return.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Steve Russell, Martin Graetz and Wayne Wiitanen conceived Spacewar while thinking about what a PDP-1 display could do. The first version was Russell’s, but the museum names Peter Samson, Dan Edwards and Graetz among those who improved it in spring 1962. Access came through MIT professor Jack Dennis. The game was therefore neither an isolated invention nor a product brief handed down by a publisher. It grew within a place where several people could try an idea, see another person’s program and decide that something needed changing.

Two ships fought around a central star whose gravity affected their movement. That arrangement made steering a problem of anticipation: a ship already moving did not simply stop because its pilot wanted a different position. Samson’s star field and the contributors’ other changes structured the scene, while the PDP-1’s input and output facilities allowed dedicated controls to join the experiment. The player’s hands, the trajectory and the display had to be considered together. Spacewar’s action came from that relationship, not merely from putting two weapons on a screen.

Decades later, the Computer History Museum began restoring a 1963 PDP-1. Volunteers first repaired and tested its power supplies so that switching it on would not damage the circuitry. It returned to life on 19 May 2004. Its account emphasizes reversible work: a repair should not needlessly destroy the evidence left by the original construction. The CPU behaved remarkably well, but the surrounding equipment demanded more attention. The route back to Spacewar began with restoring electrical reliability and careful intervention.

The processor was not enough. The restoration team also had to recover the paper-tape reader and punch, the typewriter and the display with its light pen. Those devices supplied programs and let people interact with the PDP-1. Only after the system was functioning together could the museum test software preserved in its collection. On 1 March 2005, the restored machine ran Spacewar. Later maintenance continued the work of keeping the system operational. The game could be demonstrated again because hardware repair, surviving software and knowledge of operation had been reunited.

entries.title: A game takes shape on the workbench
entries.event_semantics: Brown Box prototype period, 1968, within documented development from 1966 onward; the 1972 Odyssey is a later commercial outcome.
entries.summary: Three colleagues tested what a television could become through play.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: In 1966, Ralph Baer began exploring whether an ordinary television could be used for games. He worked at Sanders Associates, not at a company already selling home consoles. Over the following years, Bill Harrison and Bill Rusch joined the development of successive test units. The Smithsonian’s collection keeps that sequence visible: there was more than one prototype, and more than one kind of interaction to try. The Brown Box emerged from this work. Treating it as a single flash of inspiration would remove the practical experiments that made the proposal demonstrable.

The Brown Box could be configured for different games with switches. Printed cards showed which positions to use, making the control arrangement part of the experience rather than a hidden adjustment for engineers. The Smithsonian’s object interpretation connects the box to earlier units that established the basic possibility of moving a spot on a television. The team then developed more elaborate activities, including a light-gun arrangement. A prototype had to do two jobs: function on the bench and communicate its possibilities clearly enough that someone else could try it without having designed the circuit.

Baer’s Smithsonian papers include working notes, technical drawings, correspondence and audiovisual records. The finding aid also directs researchers to related collections elsewhere. These documents can connect a box to decisions made before and after it. A drawing may record an abandoned arrangement; a letter may concern licensing rather than invention. The series descriptions are a route into these differences. Reading the archive alongside the hardware prevents the surviving object from becoming a substitute for the people and negotiations behind it.

The guide distinguishes original material from later replicas and recordings of demonstrations. That matters because a working Brown Box seen today may be a reconstruction, while a period prototype can survive without being operated. The two objects answer different questions. One allows a visitor to experience the controls; the other retains physical evidence of the original work. The documented path to Magnavox’s 1972 Odyssey connects them to a commercial system, but does not make them interchangeable. Clear identification lets the museum show a playable demonstration without quietly replacing the historical artifact.

entries.title: The ruler of Lagash has to decide
entries.event_semantics: Educational development and classroom revision, 1964–1966; primary final report published June 1967. No commercial release date asserted.
entries.summary: Addis shaped an economic simulation around a pupil’s changing responsibilities.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: The 1967 project report names Mabel Addis as writer of the Sumerian Game’s instructional version and IBM’s William McKay as programmer. Its starting point was a classroom problem, not a shop shelf: children would make decisions inside a model of an ancient economy. Addis’s work supplied the situation in which those calculations would mean something. The student became Luduga, ruler of Lagash, receiving reports and deciding what to do. Writing and programming were distinct contributions to the same experience, and the contemporary report makes both names recoverable.

After an earlier group played, Addis revised the game during summer 1966. The report describes shorter, less repetitive messages and a clearer connection between economic concepts and the script. Recorded discussions among advisers broke up the reading, while charts and other visuals were made more useful to the lesson. Later stages were also reorganized to move routine calculations to the computer. The revision changed what demanded attention, giving the human more room to concentrate on the decisions the exercise was meant to teach.

The Strong’s collection contains three long teletype printouts, 39 introductory slides and the research report. A printout is a revealing survival. Instead of a screenshot of a recovered program, it records messages, responses and the changing state of a particular session. Slides preserve another part of the teaching arrangement, outside the terminal itself. The game therefore cannot be understood only as words generated by a computer. Its surviving materials show a coordinated lesson spread across paper, projected images and a pupil waiting to receive the next report.

The papers reached The Strong through donations from Devin Monnens and Alexandra Johnson; the museum subsequently added a copy of the research report. Its finding aid identifies access conditions for reference scans of the printouts. Research access is not the same as permission to redistribute each item. These limits belong to the story of what survives. The collection makes the instructional work of Addis and her collaborators visible while leaving gaps that a museum should describe, rather than fill with an invented reconstruction.

entries.title: A cartridge has to survive the living room
entries.event_semantics: Engineering of the Fairchild Channel F for its 1976 commercial introduction; later Video Soft activity is dated separately.
entries.summary: Interchangeable games required practical decisions about handling, connections and shielding.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: A removable game sounds simple once familiar. At Fairchild, it required turning Alpex’s existing idea into something that could withstand ordinary use. Jerry Lawson’s interview describes an engineering context built on earlier work. The important question was not only whether software could be changed, but whether a family could do it without damaging the system. Looking at the Channel F through Lawson’s account shifts attention from the novelty of a cartridge to the work of making a promising arrangement reliable enough for sale.

The Henry Ford’s account names Alpex engineers Wallace Kirschner and Lawrence Haskel, together with Fairchild contributors Lawson, mechanical engineer Ron Smith and industrial designer Nick Talesfore. Talesfore shaped the cartridge’s appearance, drawing on the familiar form of an eight-track tape; a protective spring-loaded door helped shield it. These were not decorative decisions added after the invention was complete. The electrical connection, the housing and the way a person handled the object had to agree. A machine with interchangeable software also needed an interchangeable object that made sense in somebody’s hand.

Lawson remembered regulatory testing as a difficult part of reaching the market. Electronic interference had to be contained, not merely ignored because the picture looked acceptable. He described surrounding the motherboard with aluminium, adding electrical bypasses to connections and placing a metal chute over the cartridge adapter. In his account, new cartridges also had to be tested. The exchange explains why commercial engineering extended beyond making a program run. The same connection that let a family change games created another opening that the team had to consider while shielding the system.

The Strong’s archival research follows Lawson beyond Fairchild. In May 1982 he incorporated Video Soft, moving from work inside a hardware company toward an independent game-development business. The company’s projects were caught in the upheaval around the market contraction and recession, and its canceled work did not establish the long commercial presence that often decides whose history is remembered. That short life still matters as a particular business attempt. It shows Lawson making another decision about where he could work and what he could build, rather than remaining permanently fixed beside the 1976 console.

entries.title: The console that left room for a computer
entries.event_semantics: APF MP 1000 console period, 1978, and the subsequent Imagination Machine expansion; no exact development or retail day asserted.
entries.summary: Smith helped connect a game console to another household possibility.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: In his Computer History Museum interview, Ed Smith began with appliances in Brownsville, Brooklyn. A repaired toaster led to other jobs, and word spread that he could make broken things work. He remembered reading, finding replacement parts and wanting to understand the electrical behaviour he encountered. This was technical learning grounded in actual objects, before he joined the team at APF. His account does not need an imposed destiny. It gives a sequence: curiosity became useful work, and useful work made a career in electronics seem possible.

At APF, Smith helped develop the MP 1000 console and the expansion that became the Imagination Machine. Benj Edwards’s published interview places him within a small engineering team, rather than describing the system as the work of one person. The possibility of expansion changes how we read the console. It could be a self-contained machine for running games, but it also formed the base of a different household computer. Smith’s story makes that junction visible. The history of home gaming included products that crossed categories instead of fitting neatly into the console or personal-computer shelf.

Smith’s own account describes the MPA-10 module joining the console to a keyboard, BASIC and a cassette recorder. Cassette material could combine program data with recorded speech, introducing software while it loaded. The controls and connections were therefore part of a proposal about what the buyer might do next. A game machine could become something to type on, learn from or program. The expansion did not erase the console beneath it. It extended an existing arrangement, using the capacity and interfaces of that machine to offer another kind of participation.

Later, Smith received requests to explain his APF work. In the 2020 oral history, he connected those inquiries with his decision to write Imagine That! The account is not a substitute for contemporary schematics or team records, but it supplies a named participant who can describe his work and question what has been omitted. A commercial ranking leaves little room for the Imagination Machine beside better-selling systems. Smith’s decision to record his experience gives the museum another measure: the knowledge of someone who helped make it.

entries.title: A river made from rules
entries.event_semantics: Development of River Raid for its 1982 publication; the feature concerns Shaw’s design process, not a birth anniversary.
entries.summary: Shaw turned a repeatable terrain sequence into a controlled challenge.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: River Raid had to provide a scrolling route within an Atari 2600 cartridge. Carol Shaw’s interview explains why the river could not simply be stored as a sequence of pictures. She used a repeatable sequence to generate terrain, then controlled what that process was allowed to produce. The method separates two things experienced together: the appearance of a continuous landscape and the rules creating it. Shaw was not merely reducing a picture until it fitted. She was deciding what information the machine actually needed to construct the flight.

Shaw’s papers at The Strong contain notes, sketches, design documents and source-code printouts. Its historical account describes Atari-era graphics drawn on graph paper and translated into numerical values, with code also written by hand before being entered. These materials preserve intermediate forms of work that a cartridge does not show. A small on-screen shape could begin as a marked square on paper; an instruction could exist first as handwriting. Following those forms makes the programmer’s decisions more visible than treating the finished display as something the computer produced alone.

Generating terrain did not settle the design. Shaw described restrictions on how narrow the river could become as the game progressed, turning an economical representation into a controlled challenge. Her conversation with Al Miller also helped move the idea away from another space setting. The aircraft, river and fuel created a different situation to read. This is where programming and design meet: the sequence supplies material, but the designer decides what kinds of passages it may produce and what the player must manage along the route.

The Strong identifies source printouts for River Raid among papers spanning Shaw’s work at Atari and Activision. The collection’s company-based arrangement places code alongside advertisements and career records. Access to some scans is managed by library staff because the connected paper requires care. A source listing is therefore instructions and an artifact that can be damaged or preserved. It gives a route toward understanding how the game was made, but its presence in an archive does not grant permission to reproduce the whole program.
